Rather than linking to heavily biased websites I will walk through this logically

The minimum wage is a topic that is constantly debated about whether or not it hurts or stimulates the economy. It seems to be one of the issues today where the easy decision to make is not always the smartest one to do. It is very easy to simply say that paying people more for their work will help the economy and the only reason that they are not paid well is because greedy corporations want more money. However, this statement is not backed by and factual data but is a form of ethos persuasion, and the minimum wage if a much more complicated issue. Let me explain.

The minimum wage is a price floor. A price floor is a legal minimum, in which the government does not allow the price of a good or service to fall below the “floor.” The motive behind these floors is that people believe that someone’s services (in this case their labor) deserve to be sold at a minimum regardless of what the market says. In most economies the minimum wage is the best example of a price floor.

The minimum wage laws are intended to benefit the people of the country by giving them higher wages and thus more money and “happiness” No one will implement any price floor if they know that it will hurt the very people it is designed to help. However, minimum wage laws have several negative (and a few positive) effects on the work force. They are as follows.

First, the minimum wage laws can and will increase unemployment in the un-skilled labor market. In every market there is an equilibrium point where the quantity demanded and supplied is equal and thus the market is at its peak potential. By having a minimum wage that is higher than the equilibrium point this will make the market less efficient. A higher wage will cause employers to cut back on their labor costs, and a higher wage will create a larger supply for labor. Thus, the supply of labor will be larger than the demand for jobs and will create a surplus of labor, also known as un-employment. As shown by the graph the equilibrium point is a 5$ per hour. At that point there are 100,000 jobs supplied and demanded, which would be 0% unemployment in theory. However at the minimum wage of 8$ employers will only demand 80,000 jobs due to the increased wage. Also, due to the higher wages there is a higher supply of labor from people that would not work for 5$. These people can be students, retires, second job workers, ect. This results in a demand of 120,000 jobs. However because there are only 80,000 jobs a shortage of 40,000 jobs ensues. So the unemployment is now at 40,000 when it was technically at zero before the price floor, even though the floor was intended for good.

Now, it is fair to point out that the 80,000 who have jobs are getting paid 3$ more than they were before. However, there are 20,000 people who would work for 5$ but can’t due to the floor. So they either go without a job, or they work under the table. If they work under the table you can imagine that their benefits and workers right would be nonexistent. They also may face tax issues in the future. So, what before had been 20,000 people with good jobs are now 20,000 people having the break the law in order to provide. So in the long run this will kill the middle class if the jobs are there only for those skilled enough the get one or desperate enough to work illegally. Not to mention that people of a higher wealth will have more relationships with industry professionals and an easier path to a job. Also, an economy with lower unemployment will always be better than one with a higher rate. And in a free economy the price of goods and services will fall to a new market price with slightly lower wages.

Second, the minimum wage laws will lower the demand for a labor in the long run. If businesses have to pay more for humans labor than they will look in other directions to get the productivity they require. For example, if the price of labor increases than companies like McDonalds or Wal-Mart will cut back on their hours, and if the minimum wage stays in place the companies will be forced to automate their processes in order to operate with less people. These improvements will cost money but in the long run they will become profitable and very hard to go without.

Finally, the minimum wage takes away a key part in the negotiation process. With a minimum in place a person cannot work for less money in order to prove themselves or establish a work history. An example is a person with no work history and who lives in a new area. It would make sense for them to be able to go to a business and offer to work for less than other people and show that they have a good work ethic. Any good business will see the potential in a good worker and offer them a higher pay so that they don’t lose them to a competitor because word will get out about the good worker. However, with a minimum the person cannot do this and is forced to find other means or work illegally with no security.

Another common argument for a higher minimum is the notion that a rising tide raises all ships. However people need the realize that prices of goods and input prices are ships as well. Example, lets look at the milk market. If their is a wage increase and the farmers pay increases, the driver pay increases, the retail pay increases, and various other pay increases than it is impossible for the milk to not increase in price as well. This combined with price increases for other goods will negate the wage increase but contribute to inflation.

An economy with no minimum wage is a very hard pill to swallow. However if people can forgot about their party lines for one second and examine the logic it becomes clear the minimum wage hurts people and the economy.

I own a small woodworking shop in the Mid-West, we do a lot of finish carpentry (Crown molding, wainscoting, chair rails, baseboards, window cornices, door and window surrounds, etc.)

When business is good, we do really well. When business is bad, we do bad. On a great month we can profit over 10K, on a bad month we can lose 10K. It's all about averages.

During the summer we do most of our work, and we hire a few high-school/college kids to haul lumber, sweep up, and just help out. We pay them MW.

If MW went up we would have to let some of them go OR (and more likely) 1099 them as private contractors where we could pay them the same rate. The fact is, what they do is not worth more than $7.50 an hour. If I were to ask any of my tradesmen or carpenters if they would rather have a gopher or make $7 more an hour, they all say "Pay me $7 more an hour and I will do all the gopher work".

My problem is I cannot lose the productivity of my skilled workers, I can't have them hauling lumber, getting everyone lunch, or doing very basic tasks, I need them working. So I hire kids to do the grunt work. But those kids are not worth $15 an hour. And if I was forced to pay them that, I wont. Not because I am a super rich ass hole, but because there is a bottom line, a bottom line that when I cross it, I don't pay my mortgage.

I believe that most people only think of McDonald's and Wal-Mart when it comes to this issue, and they forget that there are over 1,000,000 small businesses in this country with employees, and most of us owners make less than $75,000 a year. Yet we take all the risk.

Having them there is pretty much a "luxury" that isn't really needed. But if we can get it cheap enough it helps out a lot. But if we cannot get that labor cheap enough that we just don't have it and everyone else picks up the slack.

Look, you can believe whatever you wish, but if the MW in my state get's over $12 an hour, I will have less employees. The labor that my kids do is simply not worth that amount of money.

Raising MW doesn't raise prices, so I cannot charge more for my services simply because MW went up. If I cannot raise my prices, but my costs go up, I have to cut spending somewhere, and those cuts will be the unskilled labor.

I think we need to make a basic decision as a society as to whether a single person should be able to support themselves in "reasonable" fashion by working 38 / 40 hours per week and whether a person who is unable to find work but is actively trying to do so should be supported by the society as a "subsistence" level. I think they should.

Everyone that is able and willing to work should be allowed and encouraged to do so. If someone, whose abilities are not worth the mandated cost of employment, is not allowed a job, we are denying them the self respect and dignity of accomplishment. If people need assistance, before or after whatever employment that they may find, that is an entirely different issue.
